items.title: Rubio assails international court in speech to conservative legal group
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Secretary of State Marco Rubio attacked the International Criminal Court in a speech to a conservative legal group on Friday, arguing for a muscular foreign policy and against international law restraining US actions.

Rubio's speech to the Federalist Society in Washington, his first prepared remarks since Republicans were routed in the midterm elections on November 3, heightens speculation over whether he will leave his roles as national security adviser and top US diplomat to run for president in 2028.

Rubio, who has at times sought to provide an intellectual justification for President Donald Trump's "America First" foreign policy, has firmly denied reports he will soon embark on a presidential campaign, but the Federalist Society is an occasional stop for Republican hopefuls.

He has dismissed criticisms that the Trump administration has broken international law by such actions as seizing Venezuelan then-President Nicolas Maduro and striking boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific that it says were carrying drugs.

In his speech, Rubio said the goal of the US-Israeli war against Iran was to prevent Tehran from ever developing a nuclear weapon, which he said was particularly urgent because the Islamic Republic's "radical Shia clerics" had an "expansionist mentality."

He contrasted this with the government of North Korea's Kim Jong Un, whom Trump has met three times. "I'm not excusing the terrible things that have happened there," Rubio said of North Korea. "I'm just saying he (Kim) is not expansionist. He's not trying to invade Japan or, you know, China or whatever."

The US, Rubio said, would not "submit to the sterile vision of radical judges or soulless global bureaucrats," repeating his assertion that the court would try to prosecute US officials or service members that he used to justify sanctions against the ICC announced last month.

"Americans have never agreed to submit to the ICC's authority, but that court and its allies in the global bureaucracy have appointed themselves judge and jury and executioner of the international order," Rubio said.

The Trump administration has long been hostile to the Netherlands-based court, founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges. The ICC has received strong backing from most member states, which include all EU countries and all members of the NATO alliance apart from the United States and Turkey.

Washington has denounced the court over arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and an investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC says is "deprioritized."

The US sanctions, designed to stifle the ICC's ability to operate, will take effect in April unless supporters of the Netherlands-based court can reach an agreement with the US to avert them.

Rubio suggested that if the court tried to enforce its rulings against Americans, Washington would respond with force. Quoting the Roman general Pompey, Rubio said the US response would be: "Stop quoting laws to men with swords."

attachments.title: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio gives remarks at the Federalist Society's 2026 National Lawyers Convention at the Mayflower Hotel in Washington, DC, US, November 13, 2026. REUTERS/Annabelle Gordon

items.title: US loses measles-free status after continued spread of the disease, WSJ reports
items.content_html:
Nov 13 (Reuters) - The Pan American Health Organization has revoked the United States' measles-elimination status, ending a 26-year run after determining the country failed to halt continuous transmission of the highly contagious virus for more than a year, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday.

The international health body did not immediately respond to a request from Reuters for comment on the report, which cited people familiar with the matter.

The reported decision by the Americas branch of the World Health Organization comes as the US battles the highest number of measles cases it has seen in more than three decades.

Some 7,500 people in the US have been infected with measles and 13 have died since 2025. That period coincides with falling immunization rates and rising vaccine hesitancy under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has for years spread doubts, without scientific evidence, about the safety of measles vaccines.

As part of its evaluation, PAHO reviewed epidemiological and laboratory evidence submitted by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to determine whether the same strain of measles had been circulating in the United States uninterrupted for 12 months or longer, a sign of local transmission rather than imported cases.

Canada, Spain and the UK recently lost measles-elimination status after review by WHO experts. The US dropped out of WHO but remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch.

Dr Erica Schwartz, director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, told Reuters in an interview before the decision that if the US lost measles elimination, the agency would be doing "the same exact thing," which entails working with states to encourage immunization.

As of Thursday, 5,182 confirmed cases of measles had been reported in 2026 to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from 45 states, New York City and the District of Columbia, surpassing last year's total of 2,289, making it one of the country's worst measles resurgences in decades.

"It is a fully preventable disease. It is unconscionable that we have this amount of measles," said Noel Brewer, a public health professor at the University of North Carolina.

Brewer, who chairs an independent advisory panel on measles, presented the CDC's measles status report along with his group's assessment of that information to PAHO on Tuesday.

That report remains confidential, but a source familiar with the CDC's findings said the agency determined the US had 12 months of continuous transmission of the virus.

The US achieved its measles-elimination status in 2000. A country can halt transmission when 95% of its population is vaccinated, creating so-called herd immunity that also protects those unable to receive the vaccine.

Two doses of the measles vaccine — by far the best way to prevent infection and transmission — provide 97% protection against the virus, which can cause blindness, deafness, brain damage or death.

William Moss, an epidemiology professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, said loss of measles elimination was a hit to the United States' reputation as a public health powerhouse. He said it may discourage other countries.

For the average American, he added, it means that the United States will continue to have large outbreaks, putting people at risk of disease, hospitalization and death.

To restore measles-elimination status, a country must end transmission and remain free of an outbreak for at least 12 months.

The Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to a request for comment.

Reporting by Julie Steenhuysen in Chicago and Mrinmay Dey in Mexico City; Editing by Edmund Klamann, Bill Berkrot and Shri Navaratnam

items.title: Tanker collides with cruise ship in New Orleans, 32 hospitalized
items.content_html:
Nov 13 (Reuters) - A tanker ship collided with a luxury paddle wheeler docked in New Orleans on the Mississippi River on Friday, causing the cruise vessel to roll over and sink as passengers scurried to disembark and dozens were flung into the water.

All aboard the stricken ship were accounted for after harbor personnel, firefighters and onlookers scrambled to pull fallen passengers to safety, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a press conference.

Hailing the outcome as "a miracle on the Mississippi," she said 32 passengers from American Cruise Lines paddle wheeler American Heritage were hospitalized, but "none with any type of critical injuries."

Moreno said roughly 180 to 190 passengers and crew members were aboard the American Heritage at the time of the mishap. The cruise ship has a capacity for 150 passengers and was built in 2015, American Cruise Lines said on its website.

The accident occurred about midday when the tanker ship, the Atlantic Asphalt, "lost control and collided" with the docked cruise vessel, Moreno said.

As passengers began fleeing, the cruise ship started to sink and eventually "toppled over and flipped," dumping people into the river, the mayor said.

Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said about 87 passengers from the American Heritage disembarked before the vessel capsized, according to the joint news site of the New Orleans Advocate and Times-Picayune.

Moreno credited a swift response by local, state and federal personnel and bystanders from other vessels for preventing any loss of life.

The US Coast Guard said in an emailed statement that all river traffic was closed in the vicinity of the accident following the collision.

Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham told the New Orleans Advocate that the tanker appeared to have experienced some sort of steering failure but the cause of the mishap remained under investigation.

American Cruise Lines said in an emailed statement that it was coordinating with the Coast Guard and local authorities.

"Guests and crew were evacuated, and we are deeply concerned for everyone involved," the company said.

attachments.title: An American Cruise Lines passenger ship that was docked sinks in the Mississippi River after a tanker ship collided with it in New Orleans, Louisiana, November 13, 2026. Tarzan Duran/via REUTERS

items.title: Democrat Holscher wins Kansas governor's race amid data center backlash
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Democrat Cindy Holscher, who campaigned on a moratorium for data-center development, won the Kansas governor's race as the tech backlash reverberated in one of the country's most conservative states.

The state lawmaker beat her Republican rival Ty Masterson despite the state's largest transit and railroad union, as well as a local chapter of the IBEW electrical workers union, backing her opponent over the issue.

"It's the honor of a lifetime to serve as your next Governor," she wrote on X following the race call Thursday night. Masterson, a fellow state legislator, conceded the race.

Holscher's win is another example of how a Democratic candidate tapped into popular outrage around data centers and big tech, especially in rural areas. Gubernatorial candidates in Texas, Ohio, Georgia and Nevada seized on bipartisan fears about AI and data centers and pitched policies aimed at reining in the industry.

FARM BELT TURNS BLUE

The central US state also elected a Democrat for the US Senate for the first time in nearly a century, choosing pastor Adam Hamilton over incumbent Republican Roger Marshall in a backlash against Trump's immigration crackdown. It also flipped the state's attorney general, electing Democrat Chris Mann over incumbent Kris Kobach.

Holscher made data centers a central issue in her campaign, linking local anger over AI and its infrastructure to energy affordability and popular backlash against big tech.

She told Reuters earlier this year that supporting the position of a data center moratorium was a "no brainer" - because it was a top concern raised at every town hall she held across the state.

She backed the moratorium even when Democratic party officials initially advised her against it and she lost support of Kansas' top labor unions.

"What I was hearing from a lot of these folks is that they're tired of their communities being left behind in terms of economic development, but they don't want to have to sell out their resources or their people to be invested in," she told Reuters in an interview.

DATACENTER 'GUARDRAILS'

She said her moratorium would pause data center approvals until the state can get a handle on what impact they will have on the state and ensure that companies develop these projects in a way that helps, not harms communities.

"We have to have those guardrails, or it's not good for us," she said. "These big companies, some of the richest corporations in the world, can come in and steamroll some of our local city councils and our other local governing bodies."

Her opponent Masterson was supportive of data centers as a local economic driver and got backing from the state's labor unions, the first time in decades that they backed a Republican.

Kansas has been a destination for data center investment, part of a growing Midwestern technology hub dubbed the Silicon Prairie, has $46 billion in announced data center projects, primarily in the Kansas City area. Kansas is among the states targeted in a new pro-data center campaign backed by tech billionaires including Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz.

Reporting by Valerie Volcovici. Editing by Michael Learmonth

items.title: US extends shipping law waiver 90 days, to allow freer movement of oil, commodities
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump extended for 90 days a waiver of a shipping law to allow foreign-flagged ships to transport oil and other commodities between US ports, a White House official said on Friday.

Reuters reported on Thursday that industry sources said the administration would extend the waiver on the more than 100-year-old Jones Act.

It has been the longest waiver in the history of the shipping law.

The administration issued a blanket waiver in March, a month after the US launched the war on Iran, in an effort to lower oil and fuel prices. In August, it extended the waiver but mandated that decisions would be made on a case-by-case basis, a stipulation continued through the latest waiver.

The Jones Act requires cargo moving between US ports to be carried on ships built in the US, owned by US companies and crewed by American workers. Allowing the waiver aims to lower gas, diesel and fertilizer prices driven up by the war on Iran by increasing shipping flexibility and reducing transport bottlenecks.

Since the waiver was issued in March, an additional 90 million barrels of petroleum, mostly refined, have been shipped between US ports, the White House said. The total includes 27 million barrels of gasoline, 26 million barrels of crude oil, and 6 million barrels of renewable fuels.

The length of waivers has been limited in the past as the Jones Act is supported by the domestic shipbuilding business, a powerful lobby across the country.

Reporting by Timothy Gardner, Arathy Somasekhar and Jarrett Renshaw; Editing by Andrea Ricci

items.title: US to resume flights after air traffic network failure sparks chaos
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - The FAA lifted a nationwide ground stop on Friday after a communications failure at air traffic control centers caused chaos at US airports and triggered the longest shutdown since the September 11, 2001, attacks.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said US airspace reopened at 8:15 p.m. Eastern Time (0115 GMT), but warned that departures would resume gradually and it would take time for airlines to restore normal operations.

"It's going to be slow," Duffy told reporters at the White House.

By 11:30 p.m., nearly 10,000 flights had been canceled, including more than 2,200 each at Delta Air Lines and American Airlines, and 1,800 at United Airlines, according to Flightradar24. The plane-tracking website said some aircraft at major airports had waited more than five hours for a gate.

The four-hour nationwide grounding could disrupt airline schedules for days, aviation analysts said.

Duffy said tens of thousands of passengers were stranded at airports around the country. Duffy said he and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had met with President Donald Trump in the Oval Office to discuss the outage.

The failure is the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a US air traffic control system beset by aging technology, equipment and communications problems and a shortage of several thousand controllers.

Duffy said the trouble began at 3:36 p.m., when air traffic control centers experienced instability in radar and communications systems.

"Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they started to give us inconsistencies in the data from those routers and because of that we shut the system down," Duffy said, adding that at no stage did they completely lose radar or communications and they were able to safely land thousands of planes.

Duffy said the immediate problem had been fixed and that flying was safe, but warned that a broader overhaul of the aging air traffic control system was needed to prevent similar failures.

$50 BILLION AVIATION OVERHAUL

Duffy blamed Congress not funding a new system that he said could prevent such outages, and called for $50 billion to modernize it.

Earlier on Friday, before the outage, the White House and Department of Transportation had urged Congress to approve $30.1 billion to upgrade the nation's aging airports and air traffic control infrastructure.

"What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system," Duffy said. "Give us the money to fix it."

Homeland Security Secretary Mullin said there was "zero evidence" so far that the outage resulted from a cyberattack or a rogue AI system, though investigators had not ruled out either possibility.

"It appears this was mechanically driven. However, we're still looking," Mullin said.

The National Security Agency was working with the Department of Homeland Security on the investigation, he added.

The outage appeared to be affecting a telecommunications network overseen by L3Harris Technologies, according to two airline officials. The network handles critical radio frequencies used by air traffic controllers to communicate with pilots. L3Harris did not respond to a request for comment.

PAIN NOT OVER FOR PASSENGERS

Though the ground stop was lifted, the disruption for passengers was far from over. From Boston to Seattle and New York to Los Angeles, passengers crowded departure halls and airline desks as delays and cancellations mounted and aircraft remained parked at gates.

Thousands of passengers faced being stranded overnight. Edward Kargbo, 50, from West Chester, Pennsylvania, had been scheduled to take a 9 p.m. Ethiopian Airlines flight to Lomé, Togo. Instead, he planned to spend the night at the airport before a rescheduled flight at 6 a.m. on Saturday.

"I have to squat the night here," he said. "I'm stranded."

Louise Maher, 47, was also caught up in the disruption at Newark after her British Airways flight to London was disrupted by the aviation meltdown.

"I might cry at some point but not yet," she said.

US airlines will not be required to provide compensation to stranded passengers because the carriers were not responsible for the FAA system failures.

The only other nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks came in January 2023, when the FAA halted domestic departures for about 90 minutes.

Investors were already pricing in a financial hit to airlines. Shares of American (AAL.O), United (UAL.O) and Delta (DAL.N) fell between 1% and 2% in after-hours trading, while JetBlue Airways dropped about 3%.

American Airlines said it was prioritizing flights to international destinations and to smaller cities outside its major hubs to position aircraft and crews for a faster recovery.

items.title: Son of ex-CIA chief Brennan charged in child pornography case, official says
items.content_html: WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - The son of former CIA Director John Brennan was charged on Friday with transportation of child pornography, according to court documents and a US law enforcement official.

items.title: White House denies Hassett departing Trump administration
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - The White House denied on Friday that National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett was leaving the Trump administration in the coming weeks.

Earlier on Friday, Semafor, citing three people familiar with the plan, reported that Hassett was departing in the coming weeks and had been inquiring about roles outside the administration since before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which resulted in Democrats retaking both chambers of the US Congress, delivering a blow for Republican President Donald Trump.

"There is no factual basis for this reporting. Kevin Hassett is a key member of President Trump's economic team and will continue working to advance President Trump's economic policies," a White House official said.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who could hold both roles, and his counselor, David Zervos, are among the people being eyed to replace Hassett, according to Semafor. The report said Hassett's plans could change.

Semafor said Hassett's departure would be the latest in a series of staffing changes at the White House. Last week, Trump replaced his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with longtime aide Stephen Miller.

The US Treasury Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Hassett served as the chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers during Trump's first administration.

He left the role in 2019 but later returned to the White House to serve as a senior adviser to Trump during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Hassett was considered to replace Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell last year, but Kevin Warsh eventually got the role.

Reporting by Jasper Ward in Washington; Editing by Caitlin Webber

items.title: Democratic US senator probes CoreCivic sale of ICE facility in Minnesota
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - A top US Democratic senator is investigating the Trump administration's nearly half-billion-dollar purchase of a Minnesota immigration detention facility from CoreCivic (CXW.N), questioning the price and calling on the company and the Department of Homeland Security to preserve records.

"In 2025, DHS reportedly purchased the Prairie Correctional Facility from CoreCivic, a major immigration detention contractor, for $495 million — shortly after Minnesota declined to purchase the same facility for $75 million," the office of US Senator Maggie Hassan, a New Hampshire Democrat who is seeking to lead the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee when Democrats take control of Congress in January, said on Friday.

Asked about the letters — dated November 11 and made public on Friday — CoreCivic pointed to DHS and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), saying, "The federal government ultimately determined the sale price following its assessment process."

Representatives for DHS did not respond to a request for comment.

Shares of US prison operators initially fell after the Democratic sweep in US midterm elections across the country, including conservative states such as Kansas, in a major political shift seen as a backlash to Republican President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.

CoreCivic's shares, which are up about 64% so far this year, were down 3.2% on Friday afternoon in New York.

Brentwood, Tennessee-based CoreCivic, one of the largest US prison operators, with 69 correctional and re-entry facilities nationwide, and its rival, GEO Group (GEO.N), both released their third-quarter results in the days following the US midterm elections.

CoreCivic's revenue rose 28% year over year, beating analysts' expectations, as it saw increased demand from ICE and the sale of four detention facilities to the federal government for a total consideration of $2.21 billion.

The Appleton, Minnesota, facility cited by Hassan holds up to 1,600 detainees. The company announced the completion of the sale in August 2026.

CoreCivic President and CEO Lucibeth Mayberry told investors that ICE had begun to increase its enforcement activity and already had funding to continue to do so. Regarding the purchase of new detention centers, she said: "We would urge the ICE administration to move quickly."

items.title: US Air Force conducts weapons test on B-21 Raider
items.content_html:
Nov 13 (Reuters) - The US Department of the Air Force said on Friday it conducted a weapons release test for its B-21 Raider stealth bomber last week, transitioning the next-generation aircraft from flight test into a functional weapons platform.

The Air Force had awarded the development contract for the B-21, the United States' next-generation stealth bomber, to Northrop Grumman (NOC.N) in 2015.

Here are more details:

  • Northrop Grumman's partners on the B-21 program include Pratt & Whitney, Janicki Industries, Collins Aerospace, GKN Aerospace, BAE Systems (BAES.L) and Boeing (BA.N) unit Spirit AeroSystems
  • The B-21 Raider is designed to bypass dense, modern integrated air defense systems and deliver both conventional and nuclear munitions
  • During the test, a B-21 aircraft flew from Edwards Air Force Base, California, and released a conventional weapon, proving that its digital models and open systems architecture worked as expected, the Department of the Air Force said
  • "This weapons test proves the B-21 program is excelling," Air Force Chief of Staff Ken Wilsbach said
  • The Air Force said the program is ahead of schedule, with the first operational aircraft expected to arrive at Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota in 2027

attachments.title: The United States Air Force's B-21 Raider, the long-range stealth bomber that can be armed with nuclear weapons, takes off from the runway at Northrop Grumman's site at Air Force Plant 42, during its first flight, in Palmdale, California, U.S., November 10, 2023. REUTERS/David Swanson

items.title: US urges owners of 720,000 BMW vehicles to park outside over fire risks
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration urged the owners of more than 720,000 BMW (BMWG.DE) vehicles to park outside due to fire risks until repairs can be completed.

BMW said Friday it is recalling 720,796 vehicles due to a risk of fire while cars are parked and turned off. The vehicles were previously recalled in 2024 for a water pump issue and must be repaired again, NHTSA said, adding that owners "should park your vehicle outside and away from buildings and other vehicles until the vehicle is repaired."

BMW is still working on the recall fix and is aware of 10 fire incidents that may related to the issue and occurred after vehicles were repaired under the 2024 recall.

NHTSA said an improperly sealed electrical connector on the water pump may be exposed to water and short circuit, increasing fire risks.

NHTSA said the following vehicles should be parked outside until repairs can be made:

  • 2012-2016 BMW 3 Series
  • 2012-2016 BMW 5 Series
  • 2012–2015 BMW X1
  • 2012-2016 BMW Z4
  • 2013-2017 BMW X3
  • 2014-2016 BMW 2 Series coupe
  • 2014–2016 BMW 3 Series sportswagon
  • 2014-2016 BMW 328xi Gran Turismo
  • 2014-2016 BMW 4 Series convertible
  • 2014-2016 BMW 4 Series coupe
  • 2015-2016 BMW 2 Series convertible
  • 2015-2016 BMW 4 Series gran coupe
  • 2015-2018 BMW X4
  • 2016-2018 BMW X5 xDrive40e

Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Joe Bavier

attachments.title: BMW logo is seen on a vehicle at the BMW manufacturing plant in Greer, South Carolina, U.S., October 19, 2022. REUTERS/Bob Strong/File Photo

items.title: US Treasury's Bessent says he won't be cowed by death threats
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday that he would not be cowed by Iranian threats against his life, after recently moving from his Washington, DC, residence to a US military base.

"Why am I going to be afraid when our, the brave military personnel in the Gulf, President (Donald) Trump, constantly receive death threats?" Bessent said in an interview on CNBC.

Iran has denied plotting to attack officials and people on US soil.

But Bessent added that Iran was acting "like a dangerous cornered animal. So I follow Secret Service instructions and have moved from my home to a military base."

Bessent said he had to move in part because the Wall Street Journal published an aerial photo of his Georgetown home in January 2025.

"Highly irresponsible and dangerous, and things like that have to stop," he said.

A senior intelligence official in the Trump administration warned in a memo seen by Reuters late last month that Iranian plots against US personnel and American citizens had reached an advanced stage.

Bessent has led the US sanctions and economic pressure campaign against Iran, dubbed Operation Economic Outcast, since August to try to push Tehran to end attacks on shipping and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

The crucial waterway has been largely closed since the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28.

The economic pressure campaign, which coincides with a US naval blockade of Iranian ports, has included sanctions on Middle Eastern bank branches and other financial services firms facilitating transactions with Iran.

Reporting by Doina Chiacu and Katharine Jackson; Editing by Andrew Cawthorne

items.title: Trump's AI task force met Thursday, discussed AI-powered cyberattacks
items.content_html:
Nov 12 (Reuters) - Members of US President Donald Trump's AI task force met on Thursday and discussed ways to encourage critical US sectors to report AI-powered cyberattacks, according to a Trump administration spokesperson.

The task force, a group of advisers, is expected to help shape the administration's approach to AI as the technology rapidly advances.

The administration faces mounting pressure to address the risk of AI agents carrying out hacks without human authorization. OpenAI's AI agent broke out of its testing environment over the summer and attacked the AI platform Hugging Face. OpenAI and other AI firms subsequently disclosed a series of other agentic AI breakouts, often weeks or months after they occurred, and in some cases only after they were discovered by independent researchers.

Of particular concern are AI-powered cyber attacks on critical infrastructure, a term that refers to sectors vital to the US economy and security, such as banking, energy and emergency services. A cyberattack on those sectors could cause real-world danger or disruption.

Defense Department technology lead Emil Michael, who is also vice chair of the task force, talked about progress on setting national standards for AI developers to report safety incidents and share information about cybersecurity, according to the statement.

They also discussed options to encourage critical infrastructure providers to come forward with details about cybersecurity vulnerabilities and attacks without fear of legal consequences, according to the statement.

Businesses' ability to swap information about digital threats with one another and the government is underpinned by a 2015 law called the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act, which is set to expire next month. The industry sees it as a key pillar of collective digital defense because the law provides protection for defensive monitoring activities that might otherwise violate rules surrounding wiretapping or surveillance.

Reporting by Courtney Rozen and Raphael Satter in Washington; Editing by Shri Navaratnam and Thomas Derpinghaus

items.title: Chris Van Hollen announces run for US Senate majority leader, challenging Schumer
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 12 (Reuters) - Democratic US Senator Chris Van Hollen said on Thursday he would run for Senate majority leader, challenging Chuck Schumer, who has led the Democrats in the Senate since 2017, after the Democratic Party won a majority in the chamber in the midterm elections.

Schumer, who is expected to retain his party's leadership in the chamber but previously predicted not having a challenger, released his own statement on Thursday saying he had the votes to continue as the Democratic leader in the Senate.

The closed-door secret-ballot vote will take place next month.

Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, said that in the midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured a majority in the House of Representatives, voters called for "a change from the status quo that isn't working for working people."

"It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership," Van Hollen said. "That is why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader."

The 67-year-old told MSNOW in an interview he had the support of more than 10 of the 55 Democratic senators who are known to be voting but acknowledged he was the "underdog" in the race against the 75-year-old Schumer.

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, said they would support Van Hollen, who has been a US senator for nearly a decade and spent 14 years before that in the House of Representatives.

At a press conference earlier this week, Sanders and Democratic US Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan called for new leadership.

Van Hollen, who has hinted at a possible 2028 presidential campaign, has said Democrats need to simultaneously advance multiple goals, including holding President Donald Trump's administration accountable for "gross corruption," trying to end the US-Israeli war on Iran and uniting behind an aggressive economic agenda targeted at working-class Americans.

On the foreign policy front, he has been critical of Israel's occupation of Palestinian territories and its military assault on Gaza while advocating against deepening defense ties with the US ally.

"I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," Schumer said in his statement. "I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead."

A few new senators-elect have said they would not support Schumer, a Democrat from New York.

"Midterms are a referendum on the party in power, but I also think this was a plea for a new kind of politics," Van Hollen said last week, telling Reuters that Democrats should not be overly cautious in going after corporations, billionaires and special interests that voters blame for making their lives harder.

Following the midterm elections, Democrats will hold at least 55 seats in the Senate, with Republicans holding 44.

The race for a seat from Alaska has not yet been called, with the Democratic candidate holding a 2.2% lead over the Republican, with 88% of the votes counted as of late Thursday.

items.title: Gunman kills one, wounds four in busy Washington, DC, neighborhood
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 12 (Reuters) - A gunman killed one person and wounded four others in a busy Washington, DC, neighborhood on Thursday before barricading himself in his apartment and eventually taking his own life following a standoff, officials said.

The suspect, whom police identified as Matt Lambert, 55, had been embroiled in a longstanding dispute with his condominium association over mold and moisture in his apartment.

"We believe it's related to that," Metropolitan Police Interim Chief JW Carroll told a press conference on Thursday afternoon.

Police identified the dead man as James Stuart, 46, the manager of the building, and said he appeared to have been deliberately targeted.

The attack began just before 8 a.m. EST (1300 GMT) inside the gym, where police said Lambert shot and killed Stuart with a handgun before returning to his seventh-floor apartment. He then opened fire from his balcony with a rifle, striking four people, Carroll said.

Lambert also fired through his door at officers in the hallway and set a fire, according to Carroll. Police negotiators were able to speak with Lambert on the phone, but when they heard a gunshot, they forced their way into the apartment and found him dead from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Officers found three guns as well as gasoline inside the apartment.

One of the four wounded people was in critical condition, and the other three suffered non-life-threatening injuries.

SNIPERS ON ROOFTOPS

The standoff brought the normally bustling neighborhood to a standstill, as large numbers of officers in tactical gear and dozens of emergency vehicles flooded the area, shutting down streets and stationing police with rifles on rooftops.

One person who said he witnessed the incident told Reuters he heard gunshots and saw one man run to another who appeared to have been struck by a bullet.

"Blood was pouring immediately, and he said, 'He's dead,'" the witness said. "We didn't know if the gunman was still on the premises, so we just ran frantically."

Lambert, a doctor, first sued the building's condo association in 2025 over what he described as intrusive water and mold that rendered his unit unlivable. In court papers, Lambert said he had spent approximately $300,000 on remedial work.

The condo association denied the claims and filed its own countersuit against the gym that occupies the building's first floor, alleging that the facility's commercial dryers were the likely culprit. The dispute was still pending at the time of the shooting.

attachments.title: Police officers work at the site of what DC police says is a shooting, in Washington, DC, US, November 12, 2026. REUTERS/Aaron Schwartz

items.title: Hegseth awards medal to soldier who rebuked his group outside Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 12 (Reuters) - Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth awarded a medal on Thursday to a US Army sentinel who appeared to admonish him and his aides for failing to adhere to proper decorum outside the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day.

Hegseth posted a picture of him pinning a medal on Army Specialist Thomas Iglesias as he stood alongside members of his unit, the 3d US Infantry Regiment, known as The Old Guard. Hegseth wrote: "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist. Carry on Patriots."

In a video that went viral online, Iglesias on Wednesday shouted toward Hegseth, his wife and senior aides after they were seen on video taking pictures and speaking to each other on the steps of the memorial at Arlington National Cemetery following a Veterans Day event. Laughter was heard.

"All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times," Iglesias exclaimed.

Sitting at the heart of Arlington National Cemetery, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is a sacred site and the grave of three unknown American service members, including one from World War One. It is widely known as a place for mourning and for reflection on military service, and sentinels guard the site 24 hours a day.

Hegseth, a former Army National Guard soldier who served in Iraq and Afghanistan, prevailed this week when the House of Representatives rejected a Republican lawmaker's effort to impeach him.

At a rare Pentagon press conference on Tuesday hours before the vote, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a farce and defended his record, which includes championing the unpopular Iran war, launching strikes on suspected drug vessels in Latin American waters and firing senior military officers.

Democrats who won control of both chambers of Congress last week have promised to investigate Hegseth for his stewardship of the US military and have not ruled out another impeachment effort.

Reporting by Phil Stewart; Editing by Alistair Bell

items.title: Democrats prepare probes as Republicans harden ranks
items.content_html:
Nov 12 (Reuters) - The midterms may be over, but a new round of political combat in Washington is just beginning, between an emboldened Democratic-controlled Congress and a defiant White House. News tips or feedback? Send me a note: jacob.bogage@tr.com.

The election was supposed to be a contest about which party could lower the cost of living. But a week later, Washington is talking less about prices and more about investigations and looming political fights between newly empowered Democrats and the Trump administration.

Democrats are preparing a barrage of investigations into the Trump administration and have warned President Donald Trump's aides to "lawyer up." Republicans, meanwhile, are mostly elevating figures known for a more confrontational approach as they prepare to resist what promises to be much tougher Democratic oversight of the Trump administration.

Trump has chosen Stephen Miller, one of the most divisive figures in his administration, as his new chief of staff. In the House of Representatives, Republicans elected Jim Jordan of Ohio, a former wrestling coach known for his bare-knuckle politics, as their next leader, ejecting a longtime party fixture, Louisiana Representative Steve Scalise, from leadership.

Republicans in the Senate re-elected South Dakota Senator John Thune as their leader, but several lawmakers tried to delay the proceedings to allow a challenger to emerge. Trump has clashed with Thune and accused him of delaying elements of the White House's agenda. After he was re-elected, Thune pledged to "be very, very active in asserting conservative priorities" when Democrats take control in January.

Democrats are seeking probes into the Iran war, Trump's immigration agenda and his handling of spy agencies. They are also openly discussing another impeachment attempt of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and one into Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The White House warned that Democrats' investigations could venture into criminal activity, a threat lawmakers largely shrugged off.

As lawmakers duel on Capitol Hill, Republicans and Democrats are gathering at a series of conferences to debate the future direction of their parties. Progressives huddled at "Crooked Convention," organized by Crooked Media in Washington, where activists argued the election vindicated their policies. More moderate Democrats will gather for three days in Denver from today to discuss how to bring the two major factions of the party together ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

Republicans spent part of the week at "The Forum" in Maryland, assessing what went wrong. I was there, and the conversation was blunt.

"With all due respect to the political operation in the White House, you messed up," said retiring Texas Representative Chip Roy. "You went around the country saying, 'I want more power.'"

Roy's criticism reflects the debate underway in both parties about what lessons to draw from the midterms and how best to appeal to voters unhappy with the country's direction. With 2028 potential candidates already starting to emerge, that debate will only intensify. Expect the elbows to keep flying in Washington and beyond.

TOP US POLITICS HEADLINES

  • White House tells Democrats that investigating Trump administration could be criminal
  • After midterm rout, Vance tries to build his own 2028 brand
  • Kennedy family tries to stop Trump's Washington arch
  • US Senate to take up energy permitting bill votes next week, Whitehouse says

THE VIEW FROM TAPACHULA, MEXICO

More than 1,000 migrants were walking northward on Wednesday in a caravan through southern Mexico, spurred by last week's Democratic victory in US midterm elections, which raised hopes that US immigration policies could become more welcoming. The group, estimated by a Chiapas state government source to number about 1,500 people including many families, set off on Tuesday from the city of Tapachula near the Guatemala border. With possessions in backpacks, parents carried small children in their arms, in strollers, or on their shoulders.

WHAT TO WATCH FOR

November 12-14: Democrats gather in Denver for "What's Next" convention

November 16: Trump travels to the Philippines for ASEAN summit

November 18-19: Trump attends the APEC summit and meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China

THE WHO, WHAT AND WHEN

  • How much does it cost to lose the Senate?
  • Democratic attorney general wins could reshape US lawsuits on abortion, immigration and more
  • Can a new Congress mean an end to the Iran war?
  • All midterm results in maps and charts

Reporting by Jacob Bogage, Editing by Ross Colvin and Alistair Bell

items.title: US House Democratic Leader Jeffries wants 'dramatic change' in Middle East
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 12 (Reuters) - US House of Representatives Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries called on Thursday for "dramatic change" in the Middle East and reiterated his support for a two-state solution for Israel and the Palestinians.

Democrats' sweeping victories in last week's midterm elections could lead to the curbing of US support for its close ally Israel, putting the spotlight on party leaders' views as they prepare to take control of both houses of Congress on January 3.

Jeffries, a New York Democrat, is expected to be the next House speaker.

"The status quo is unacceptable, and we need dramatic change. And that looks like, as far as I'm concerned, making sure you have a safe and secure Israel, living side by side as a Jewish and democratic state with an independent Palestinian state that provides dignity and self-determination for the Palestinians," he said at a weekly press conference.

Next year, Democratic leaders will have the lead in writing bills and deciding what legislation comes up for a vote, although Republican President Donald Trump retains the power to veto measures passed by Congress. It takes two-thirds majorities in both the House and Senate to overcome a veto.

Many of the winning Democrats had campaigned against military aid to Israel and the US-Israeli war with Iran, issues expected to get greater scrutiny in Congress next year.

Washington has historically supported a negotiated two-state solution, although the Trump administration has focused on its own plan for Gaza and a broader Middle East settlement.

The steep toll on civilians of Israel's campaign in Gaza and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's embrace of Trump and other Republicans had already strained decades of bipartisan support for Israel.

Jeffries called for "dramatic change" in the West Bank, Gaza and to the Memorandum of Understanding with Israel, which provides $3.8 billion in US military aid to Israel each year and expires in September 2028.

Reporting by Patricia Zengerle; Editing by Jonathan Spicer

items.title: White House set to extend Jones Act shipping waiver, sources say
items.content_html:
HOUSTON/WASHINGTON Nov 12 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's administration is set to extend a waiver to a US law in coming days allowing some foreign-flagged ships to transport oil and other commodities between US ports, four industry sources said on Thursday.

The extension will require individual voyages to undergo case-by-case review rather than allowing foreign ships to receive blanket exemptions from the Jones Act, two sources said. The waiver is one of the tools the administration has used to try to lower diesel and gasoline prices, which have been driven higher by the wars in Iran in Ukraine.

The waiver could come as early as Thursday, one of the sources said. The administration last extended the waiver in August until November 15, and it has already been the longest waiver in history for the more than 100-year old law.

A White House official said no decision has yet been made on the extension of the Jones Act waiver, adding that any announcements will be made directly Trump or his administration.

The Jones Act requires cargo moving between US ports to be carried on ships built in the US, owned by US companies and crewed by American workers, and the waiver aims to lower gas prices by increasing shipping flexibility and reducing transport bottlenecks.

While the Jones Act waiver increases the availability of tankers to move fuel, it would likely only reduce gasoline prices by pennies per gallon, some analysts and industry experts have said.

About 300 waivers were provided under the blanket Jones Act waivers in March and May, while about 48 waivers have been provided under the exemptions from August, which had limited the scope of the waivers, data from the administration showed.

US gasoline prices averaged about $3.91 on Thursday, compared with $2.98 before the US-Iran war, while diesel prices have risen to $6.10 versus $3.76 before the war, according to data from AAA.

(This story has been refiled to remove extraneous words from the headline.)

Reporting by Jarrett Renshaw and Arathy Somasekhar; Editing by Timothy Gardner and Chizu Nomiyama

items.title: US labor market resilient; existing home sales hit more than 16-year low in October
items.content_html:
• Weekly jobless claims increase by 9,000 to 200,000
  • Continuing claims decline by 20,000 to 1.697 million
  • Existing home sales drop 5.5% to 3.75 million units, lowest level since August 2010
  • Median existing house price rises 0.4% from a year ago to $421,900

WASHINGTON, Nov 12 (Reuters) - The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits increased more than expected last week, but remained at a level consistent with a stable labor market, allowing the Federal Reserve to focus on fighting inflation.

Economists expect layoffs to remain low through the end of the year, though seasonal volatility related to the holiday season could cause some spikes in the claims data. The government last week reported a surge in nonfarm payrolls in October and a decline in the unemployment rate to 4.1% from 4.2% in September. The resilience in the labor market is despite the ongoing Middle East conflict, which is boosting inflation.

"Firms are continuing to hold on to labor," said Olivia Cross, senior US economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics. "We expect layoffs to remain low through the fourth quarter, but then come under some pressure next year in response to the recent tightening of financial conditions and the growing use of AI by firms."

Initial claims for state unemployment benefits rose 9,000 to a seasonally adjusted 200,000 for the week ended November 7, the Labor Department said on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 195,000 claims for the latest week.

Claims have stayed at or below 200,000 since mid-September and remain close to the 189,000 level touched in mid-July, the lowest since 1969, raising the prospect that the labor market could be tightening. But with wages growing at a moderate pace, most economists do not believe that is the case.

Some argue that a smaller workforce, due to retirements and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, is the key driver of the historically low level of claims.

"A generally smaller labor force could mean fewer workers to file for unemployment insurance," said Veronica Clark, an economist at Citigroup. "Of course, this would still be consistent with a low unemployment rate, with continuing claims suggesting the unemployment rate may even fall further towards around 4.0% in data by early 2027."

The claims report showed that the number of people receiving unemployment benefits after an initial week of aid, a proxy for hiring, fell 20,000 to a seasonally adjusted 1.697 million during the week ended October 31. But the so-called continuing claims do not include some unemployed people, such as recent college graduates and others who have little or no work history.

Some people might also have exhausted their eligibility for benefits, limited to 26 weeks in most states, keeping continuing claims at relatively low levels. The median duration of unemployment jumped to 11.9 weeks in October, the longest since November 2021, from 11.5 weeks in September.

Though businesses have been hoarding workers, they have remained reluctant to increase headcount, with economists citing uncertainty from the US-Israeli war with Iran, now in its ninth month. Businesses were also unsure of their staffing needs as they embraced AI.

US central bank Governor Michael Barr warned on Thursday the nation should be prepared for "serious short-term disruptions" to the job market because of AI, which he said, depending on how fast it is deployed, could begin displacing workers at scale and widening inequality in favor of investors.

Stocks on Wall Street were trading lower as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's exit and rising oil prices following comments by President Donald Trump that the US did not need a deal with Iran weighed on sentiment. The dollar advanced against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields rose.

HOUSE PRICES STILL ELEVATED

Government data this week showed consumer prices increasing faster than expected in October. That, together with comments from Fed Governor Christopher Waller, prompted financial markets to almost fully price in a 25-basis-point rate hike in December, and to anticipate another increase in January.

The Fed left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range last month. While the labor market continues to hold up, rising mortgage rates stemming from the Iran war are depressing the interest-rate-sensitive housing market.

Sales of previously owned homes tumbled 5.5% in October to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million units, the National Association of Realtors said in a separate report. That was the lowest level since August 2010, when sales were declining as a homebuyers tax credit ended. The incentive was aimed at stimulating demand following the 2008 global financial crisis.

Economists had forecast home resales falling to a rate of 3.85 million units. Sales plunged 8.8% on a year-over-year basis in October. The drop in sales was across all price categories, including those priced $1 million and above, which had experienced strong growth in prior months.

The 30-year fixed mortgage rate jumped above 7% in late August, rising to 7.40% by mid-September, for a total of 142 basis points since the US and Israel attacked Iran at the end of February, data from mortgage finance agency Freddie Mac showed.

It averaged 7.11% in the latest week, down from 7.18% in the prior week.

"Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023," said Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist.

The NAR's Housing Affordability Index dropped to 100.7 from 107.3 in October 2025.

Existing housing inventory increased 1.3% to 1.590 million units, the highest level since November 2019. Supply rose 4.6% from a year ago. At October's sales pace, it would take 5.1 months to exhaust the current inventory of existing homes, the most since November 2015. That was up from 4.4 months a year ago. The median existing home price last month advanced 0.4% from a year ago to $421,900, the highest for any October.

First-time buyers accounted for 29% of sales, down from 32% a year ago. A 40% share in this category is needed for a robust housing market. The housing market weakness is demand-related, with higher prices keeping distressed sales at a negligible 2%.

"With mortgage rates expected to remain above 7% through most of 2027, we expect home sales to remain below 4 million until late next year," said Nancy Vanden Houten, lead US economist at Oxford Economics.

Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama, Paul Simao and Andrea Ricci

items.title: USPS plans 11% package fuel surcharge but no first-class stamp hike
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 12 (Reuters) - The cash-strapped US Postal Service said on Thursday it is seeking approval for an 11% price hike for domestic priority mail and package deliveries in January to deal with rising fuel costs.

USPS, which needs approval from the Postal Regulatory Commission for the price increase, said it was not planning to hike the price of first-class stamps in January, which rose in July from 78 to 82 cents.

The surcharge is rising from a temporary 8% surcharge that was imposed in April. USPS said this week its transportation expenses in the 12 months ending September 30 rose by $225 million due to higher fuel costs.

USPS said it was proposing to hike overall domestic shipping services prices 5.9% on average and is raising prices by an average of 7.9% for international deliveries.

USPS asked Congress on Tuesday for $2 billion in support and reimbursements as its head warned the agency would be forced to make significant cuts in retail post offices and other reductions unless lawmakers act.

USPS reported an annual $6.5 billion loss versus a net loss of $9 billion in the prior 12 months.

The new Democratic-led Congress, which takes office in January, will need to decide whether to help the Postal Service after Republicans held a series of hearings over the last two years on its finances. USPS wants $2 billion from Congress for unfunded requirements it has imposed.

The agency has recorded net losses of more than $120 billion since 2007. The volume of first-class mail, its most profitable product, fell this year to its lowest level since 1965 as consumers have moved to digital communication, while USPS must still pay for costly nationwide delivery.

Postmaster General David Steiner says the agency has a broken business model and needs help from lawmakers to turn around its operations.

In May, USPS suspended non-essential spending on travel, office supplies and consultants. USPS also earlier this year temporarily suspended employer payments for a federal pension program.

Reporting by David Shepardson in Washington; Editing by Bill Berkrot

items.title: Florida city says it will not host St Patrick's Day parade, Pride event due to anti-diversity law
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 11 (Reuters) - A city in Florida said it will not host its annual St. Patrick's Day Parade or Pride event in 2027 due to a state law signed by Republican Governor Ron DeSantis that prohibits local governments from promoting or funding diversity initiatives.

The city of Delray Beach said in a statement that restrictions under the law "include certain programming and activities designed or implemented with reference to ethnicity, sexual orientation, or gender identity."

Mayor Tom Carney said on social media the city was "working feverishly with multiple entities to ensure the 2027 St. Patrick's Day parade goes on as scheduled."

St. Patrick's Day in March honors Ireland's patron saint and Irish culture and heritage. Pride festivals celebrate LGBTQ communities.

The bill was signed by DeSantis in April and takes effect on January 1.

Republican state leaders and US President Donald Trump's administration have rallied against diversity, equity and inclusion practices, casting them as discriminatory against groups like white people and men.

At the federal level, Trump has signed executive orders aimed at dismantling such initiatives and has threatened to freeze funds for educational institutions over diversity programs.

Civil rights advocates say diversity initiatives help address historic inequities for marginalized groups like the LGBT community, women and ethnic minorities.

DeSantis says the law requires grant recipients to certify that public funds will not be used to advance such initiatives and provides enforcement mechanisms, including penalties for officials who violate the law.

Last week, the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the largest US Muslim advocacy group, suspended operations in Florida after the enforcement of a separate law that gave state officials power to designate groups as "terrorist organizations."

items.title: Trump threatens to double tariffs on Mexico if it does not halt migrants
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 12 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump threatened on Thursday to double tariffs on Mexico if it does not stop more than a thousand migrants walking north toward the United States after last week's US election, warning that they would not be allowed to enter.

"Here we go again!" the Republican president wrote on social media. "They will not be accepted! MEXICO MUST STOP THEM, NOW, and if they do not do so, the Tariffs on Mexico will be IMMEDIATELY DOUBLED. MEXICO, THE GOVERNOR OF TEXAS, THE VERY LIBERAL NEW GOVERNOR OF TEXAS, OUR GREAT BORDER PATROL, & ICE, HAVE BEEN SO INFORMED. There will be no leniency!"

An estimated 1,500 people, mostly from Central America, set off on Tuesday from the southern city of Tapachula near the Guatemalan border. The migrants are hoping that the election victory by Democrats that gives the party control of Congress starting in January could open pathways for them to live and work in the United States.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum recognized that a group of people were walking northward toward the United States, but said that no migrant caravans have arrived at the US border since Trump returned to power last year.

People in the migrant caravan have been informed of how difficult it is to enter the US, and Mexico is looking to return them to their countries of origin, Sheinbaum told a regular press conference.

"There will be no acts of repression," Sheinbaum added.

Some local media have reported that authorities in the southern state of Chiapas have turned back migrants as they sought to join the group this week.

Mexico's migration institute and the Chiapas state government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

"We will utilize all assets to make sure our borders are secure," US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote on social media following Trump's tariff threat. "This illegal migrant caravan will NOT be allowed to enter our country. Full stop."

The United States and Mexico are negotiating a trade agreement after Trump chose in July to not extend the US-Mexico-Canada trade pact.

The Trump administration's tough immigration policies mostly stopped the flow of migrants to the US southern border, leaving many Mexican migrant shelters empty.

Trump was elected to a second term as president in 2024 in part over concern among US voters about the border. Since then, Trump has highlighted some migrant caravans but also said in recent months the issue has become less politically potent for him and his fellow Republicans.

"I am sure the new governor is going to want to have security at the Texas border," Trump told reporters after the November 3 midterm election, referencing the newly elected Texas governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

Trump also has acknowledged political backlash from his administration's deportation program through US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

On Sunday, Trump told the CBS program "60 Minutes" that the deportation force had been "too tough" and that he was open to making an immigration deal with Democrats after they take control of Congress.

items.title: Trump says US does not need Iran deal, directs Vance to focus on domestic corruption
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 12 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Thursday the US does not need a deal with Iran and directed Vice President JD Vance, who has played a role in efforts to resolve the war, to focus "his complete and total attention" on alleged crime and corruption in Democratic-run cities and states.

Trump's directive came a day after the Wall Street Journal reported that Vance was considering face-to-face peace talks with a hard-line Iranian security official and a week after the vice president blamed the costly war with Iran for Republicans' midterm elections drubbing.

"We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!" Trump wrote on social media, referring to the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump had suggested in recent weeks that Iran would be more willing to strike a deal in the eight-month conflict after the US elections, but his administration this week signaled it believes its blockade and economic sanctions against Iran are working, meaning neither a military escalation nor diplomacy is needed.

The US military is imposing a blockade on Iranian ports, while attempting to secure safe passage for international shipping through the vital Strait of Hormuz. Iran's military said on Thursday four oil tankers were hit by explosions after they ignored Iranian warnings.

Vance's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

VANCE HAD LED IRAN DIPLOMACY

Vance, long seen as skeptical of the war the US and Israel launched on Iran in February, led talks with Iranian officials in Pakistan in April that produced a June memorandum of understanding that paused the war but broke down within weeks.

Iranian state media said late last month Tehran had received a letter from Vance seeking renewed talks with Washington. Trump said he had not directed his vice president to make the outreach.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday after talks with US allies in Paris that Iran's demands for a potential deal were "absurd," citing its demand for reparations for the war, and said Trump would not sign a bad deal.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that Vance was considering meeting with a senior Iranian security official, a move that would have put Vance at the center of peace negotiations. Reuters has not confirmed the potential talks.

Vance, who is viewed as a leading contender for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, distanced himself from the war last week after Republicans' midterm election rout by Democrats.

The vice president blamed the costs of the Iran war in part for the party's losses. He also said an earlier recommendation to end the war was "sound advice."

Trump responded to Vance's position by defending the war as necessary to stop Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

In his social media post, Trump said he had asked Vance to focus instead on a domestic issue the president previously put in his portfolio: leading an effort targeting alleged fraud in Democratic-run cities and states throughout the US.

"Our Budget could be quickly BALANCED with the correction of this large-scale criminal activity. CORRUPTION is in the Democrat Leadership's blood!" Trump wrote on Thursday.

Reporting by Bo Erickson in Washington; additional reporting by Simon Lewis, Doina Chiacu and Susan Heavey. Editing by Colleen Jenkins, Andrea Ricci, Don Durfee and Nia Williams

items.title: Vance, Rubio, Ossoff and Buttigieg lead 2028 White House hopefuls, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
items.content_html:
Summary:

  • Rubio gets excellent-candidate rating from 45% of Republicans, just ahead of Vance's 43%
  • Ossoff and Buttigieg each get excellent-candidate ratings from 29% of Democrats
  • Reuters/Ipsos surveyed 1,705 US adults and showed 5-point margins of error by party

WASHINGTON, Nov 12 (Reuters) - Four potential contenders in the 2028 race for the White House have caught American voters' attention with their early jockeying: Republicans JD Vance and Marco Rubio and Democrats Jon Ossoff and Pete Buttigieg, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll.

None of the four has yet formally launched a campaign and the parties' 2028 nominating contests are more than a year away, leaving plenty of time for new contenders to emerge and for voters' views to change.

Some 45% of Republican voters polled said they believed Secretary of State Rubio would be an "excellent" presidential candidate, with 43% saying the same of Vice President Vance. Former Transportation Secretary Buttigieg and US Senator Ossoff, of Georgia, each got that rating from 29% of Democratic voters.

The poll, which surveyed 1,705 US adults nationwide including roughly 500 registered voters from each party and was completed on Monday, had a margin of error of 5 percentage points for Republican and Democratic voters.

President Donald Trump, struggling with an approval rating near the lowest of his career, looms large over the conversation for both parties. Republicans are divided on whether they want a candidate who breaks with Trump or follows in his footsteps, while Democrats, who are flying high after routing Republicans in the November 3 congressional elections, are divided on how aggressively to go after the president, such as through impeachment.

Trump has quizzed allies on whom they prefer Vance or Rubio and in a Sunday interview with CBS's "60 Minutes" said he would "not necessarily" make an endorsement in the Republican primary.

'MANAGED TO DO HIS JOB'

Barbara Rezner, an attorney in Florida who voted for Trump in the last three presidential elections, said she prefers Rubio over Vance, whom she considers too far to the right and too close to the president.

"Rubio has managed to do his job. He's stayed off most people's radar because he hasn't done anything too far left, too far right, too crazy," Rezner said.

The modest but growing dissatisfaction with Trump among Republicans is centered on the president's decision to launch a war on Iran that has driven fuel prices higher. Rubio has been notably absent from many of the so-far fruitless peace talks with Iran despite being the nation's top diplomat. Vance has shown signs of wanting to distance himself as well, saying publicly that the Republican drubbing in the midterm elections owed to the war with Iran.

A dozen-odd other Republicans are also in the national conversation over 2028 contenders, with Florida Governor Ron DeSantis among the best regarded, with 32% of Republicans rating him as an excellent option. Others - like Trump's son, Donald Trump Jr., and Texas US Senator Ted Cruz - have their fans, but also many detractors.

OSSOFF AND BUTTIGIEG

Among Democrats, Ossoff is at the top of many voters' lists, with 29% of the party's registered voters rating him as excellent. Ossoff has grabbed headlines in recent months by calling Trump corrupt and unfit for office in unusually direct language, and last week he won his re-election race by 18 percentage points in Georgia, a state Trump carried by 2 points in 2024.

Buttigieg also gets the excellent rating from 29% of Democrats. Buttigieg also ran for president in 2020 and is better known nationally than Ossoff.

About one in five Democrats say they have never heard of Buttigieg, compared to roughly one in three who say the same about Ossoff. Very few Republicans are unfamiliar with Vance, but about one in six said they do not know who Rubio is. For candidates in either party, starting the election cycle with more name recognition can save money that would be spent getting the candidate's name out, but examples abound of little-known candidates catching fire during the campaign, as happened with former President Bill Clinton.

Buttigieg and Ossoff are considered moderates among Democrats, and that appeals to Democratic voters like Ed Blair, a retired pig farmer in southern Illinois, who gives Buttigieg a better rating in part because Ossoff is less familiar.

"I do favor the more moderate candidates over the more progressive ones," said Blair, who is wary of proposed major shifts like expanding federal Medicare health insurance coverage from all seniors to everyone in the country. Blair would prefer gradual shifts, such as expanding Medicare to cover all children. "In going towards some of the progressive policies, small steps need to be taken rather than large ones to give people time to adapt."

The Reuters/Ipsos poll shows other well-known moderates - like former Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost to Trump in the 2024 presidential election, and California Governor Gavin Newsom - each get "excellent candidate" ratings of 23%, higher than the 15% of Democrats who view progressive stalwart Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a US representative for New York, that way.

Ocasio-Cortez told CNN after the midterms that impeaching Trump should be an option on the table, while Buttigieg told the New Yorker magazine he is "not very interested" in impeachment.

Elaine Kamarck, a Democratic strategist, cautioned against reading too deeply into the public's current views this far out from the 2028 election. "It's a world away," Kamarck said. "There are lots of people in both parties who are still deciding if they are going to run. You might be able to predict who will run, but you certainly don't know anything about who is going to be ahead."

Reporting by Tim Reid and Jason Lange; Editing by Scott Malone and Alistair Bell

items.title: Can a new US Congress mean an end to the Iran war?
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, November 12 - The American public wants the unpopular eight-month-long war on Iran to end, and showed it by handing President Donald Trump's Republicans a resounding defeat in last week's congressional elections.

Trump acknowledged that unhappiness about the conflict contributed to his party's losses, but defends the war, both insisting that he has won it and saying it will continue.

Congress cannot unilaterally end the war, but can pressure the president to do so.

Here are some ways lawmakers in the new Congress — which is scheduled to be sworn in on January 3 — can push to end the fighting.

MONEY TALKS, AS DO SHUTDOWNS

Under the US Constitution, Congress decides how federal funds should be spent. Trump has asked the House of Representatives and Senate to approve a huge increase in the defense budget — from about $950 billion to $1.5 trillion, plus an additional $67 billion for the war.

Democrats say they will not approve such a massive budget next year. But they also have proposed cutting off funding for the war even before the new Congress is seated, suggesting that anti-war Republicans or fiscal hawks concerned about the deficit might back them.

The current government funding bill expires on December 11, meaning Congress must pass a full-year budget or a short-term spending plan to avoid a shutdown right before Christmas, interfering with travel and putting thousands out of work.

House Republican leaders say the party will hold firm behind Trump.

"A Republican Congress is not going to send bills to a Republican president that he's going to veto, so if that's their (the Democrats') demand, well, we'll just wait until next year," Representative Tom Cole of Oklahoma, who chairs the House Appropriations Committee, told reporters this week.

But once the Democrats control Congress, they can include clauses in budget bills forbidding the use of any funds for hostilities against Iran. Trump could issue vetoes, but would again risk a government shutdown, and potentially no pay for the troops themselves, in order to prolong the war.

Congress can also refuse to authorize any funding for the war in the annual National Defense Authorization Act, or NDAA, which sets policy for the Pentagon. Since the NDAA has passed every year since 1961, its failure would be an embarrassment for both parties.

LEGISLATION

Trump did not secure approval from Congress before he launched the war alongside Israel on February 28, and Democrats, along with a few Republicans, have voted repeatedly to end the fighting unless he seeks congressional authorization.

One of these war powers resolutions passed both the House and Senate, but Trump's administration ignored it, and legal experts said there is no consensus on whether it was binding.

Democrats have vowed to keep pushing, and expect votes on more war powers resolutions, with more legislation promised once they control the House and Senate.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll this month showed 71% of Americans — including 93% of Democrats and 51% of Republicans — want Congress to pass legislation ending the conflict.

Trump is expected to veto any measure to stop the fighting. It takes two-thirds majorities in both chambers to override a veto, meaning Democrats would need Republican support to overcome Trump's objections.

However, backers say it is worth trying, to send a message to Trump, and the American public, that many members of Congress want the fighting to stop.

They also say that sentiments might change, even among Republicans, if the war drags on.

OVERSIGHT

An effort led by Republican Representative Thomas Massie and backed mainly by Democrats to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on charges including waging the Iran war without congressional approval failed this week. But Democrats may try again next year, viewing Hegseth as the individual most responsible for the war, after Trump.

Once they are in charge of congressional committees, Democrats can hold hearings and launch investigations into the Trump administration's strategy, spending and conduct of the war. And they will have the power to issue subpoenas to compel testimony.

Individual members of Congress and Democrats on congressional committees have already been sending letters to the State and Defense departments asking for the preservation of documents associated with decision-making on the war.

If the administration refuses to cooperate with such inquiries, Congress can apply pressure, such as by withholding funding for officials' travel budgets or, in the case of the Senate, by declining to confirm Trump's nominees.
